facts.claim: The Awakening Conscience, oil on canvas, 1853, by William Holman Hunt (1827–1910); Tate Britain, London (T02075); 76.2 × 55.9 cm; presented by Sir Colin and Lady Anderson 1976; on display in Room 10

At first glance it may look like a young married couple, or a brother and sister; but she is his mistress (half dressed, no wedding ring); The woman's left hand shows the absence of a wedding ring, although rings are worn on every other finger
Annie Miller, the model, was an uneducated barmaid whom Hunt met in 1850 when she was fifteen; she lived/worked in Chelsea
Hunt tried to 'rescue' and educate Annie Miller to make her his wife; the face we see now was repainted later by Hunt
Hunt was one of the founders of the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood (1848) with Millais and Rossetti, a rebellion against the Royal Academy's teaching

In 1851, with The Light of the World on his easel at Chelsea, Hunt thought his spiritual subject called for 'a material counterpart' showing how 'the appeal of the spirit of heavenly love calls a soul to abandon a lower life' (Hunt's memoir). Tate notes Hunt dated the idea 1851 in his first edition and 1853 in his second
The Light of the World shows Christ at night knocking at a door overgrown with weeds and ivy, never opened (Ruskin's description reprinted by Hunt)

Hunt: in reading David Copperfield he had been deeply touched by old Peggotty's search for little Emily when she had become an outcast, and 'went about to different haunts of fallen girls to find a locality suitable'
The verse from Proverbs 25:20 led him to the subject: 'As he that taketh away a garment in cold weather, so is he that singeth songs to an heavy heart'; it is on the frame
Hunt's idea: 'the companion of the girl's fall might himself be the unconscious utterer of a divine message', his song stirring her memories while he 'still sings on'
Augustus Egg talked about Hunt's design to the Manchester businessman Thomas Fairbairn, who commissioned the picture; to paint it Hunt deferred his journey to the East
Hunt hired a room at Woodbine Villa, 7 Alpha Place, St John's Wood, a 'maison de convenance' (where men kept their mistresses), as the setting

Ruskin on the room: everything new — the rosewood furniture's 'terrible lustre', 'its fatal newness', nothing 'that has the old thoughts of home upon it', the embossed books 'marked with no happy wearing of beloved leaves'
facts.source: https://archive.org/details/preraphaelitism01hunt (vol. I pp. 418–19, Ruskin's letter to The Times, 25 May 1854) ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Awakening_Conscience

facts.claim: The picture was begun by February 1853 and completed in January 1854, when Hunt left for the Middle East

Hunt: the dark weather delayed his finishing; he waited for one bright day; 'by four o'clock I had accomplished all'; he left that night by the mail train, and Millais, seeing him off at the station, rushed to the buffet for food because he had not had time to dine; Annie Miller was born in 1835 in Chelsea; her father Henry had been a soldier in the 14th Dragoons, wounded in the Napoleonic Wars
Hunt found her at a pub near his studio; he arranged for her to learn to read and to take lessons in deportment, intending to marry her; he planned to marry her after her schooling
Hunt was deeply religious; he went to the Holy Land to paint biblical subjects truthfully
Before leaving in 1854, Hunt arranged for her education and left money for her upkeep and a list of artists (including Millais) she could sit for
Hunt definitely did not want Annie to sit for Rossetti (Nahum: 'strictly forbade her to model for other artists, in particular Rossetti'); hedged as 'the story goes'

The painting is meant to be 'read': a cat toying with a broken-winged bird under the table symbolises the woman's plight; A man's discarded glove warns that the likely fate of a cast-off mistress was prostitution (Tate)

A tangled skein of yarn (wools of an unfinished tapestry) on the floor symbolises the web in which the girl is entrapped; The clock on the piano is encased in a glass dome; Tate's label: 'the female figure enclosed in a glass dome'
On the floor: the sheet music of Edward Lear's setting of Tennyson's 'Tears, Idle Tears'; on the piano: Thomas Moore's 'Oft in the Stilly Night', whose words speak of sad memories of a happier past
The mirror behind her reflects the sunlit spring garden she gazes at through the window
The frame, designed by Hunt: bells and marigolds for warning and sorrow, a star above her head as a sign of spiritual revelation
Hunt's original title was 'The still small voice'; it was Thomas Combe (Hunt's patron in Oxford) who suggested 'The Awakening Conscience'

Both paintings were exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1854 (The Awakening Conscience no. 377, The Light of the World no. 508); reviews appeared from 29 April; Athenaeum 1854: 'Innocent and unenlightened spectators suppose it to represent a quarrel between a brother and sister'; and 'The author of "The Bridge of Sighs" could not have conceived a more painful-looking face'; Morning Chronicle, 29 April 1854: 'This is an absolutely disagreeable picture'
facts.source: https://web.archive.org/web/2008/http://www.tate.org.uk/servlet/ViewWork?cgroupid=-1&workid=6996&searchid=false&roomid=false&tabview=text&texttype=8 ; https://archive.org/details/preraphaelitism01hunt (vol. I pp. 405–6) ; https://archive.org/details/preraphaelitism01hunt (vol. I p. 405) ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Awakening_Conscience ; https://archive.org/details/preraphaelitism01hunt (vol. I p. 406)

facts.claim: 'The Bridge of Sighs' is Thomas Hood's poem about a woman who drowns herself in the Thames; Ruskin's letter to The Times, 25 May 1854: 'People gaze at it in a blank wonder, and leave it hopelessly'; her face: 'the lips half open… the eyes filled with the fearful light of futurity and with tears of ancient days'
Ruskin: 'There is not a single object in all that room, common, modern, vulgar …, but it becomes tragical, if rightly read'
Ruskin had defended the Pre-Raphaelites before (letters to The Times, 1851) and defended this picture and the PRB
Hunt read Ruskin's letters in the Holy Land: 'It could not but gratify and encourage me to read these words'

While Hunt was away, Annie sat for Millais (on the approved list), and against Hunt's wishes for George Price Boyce and for Rossetti; She accompanied Rossetti and Boyce to restaurants and for walks in the park, and went to the Cremorne pleasure gardens, where she danced with Boyce
Hunt returned from his travels in 1856; on discovering this he declared 'I will never forgive Gabriel' (Fleming, quoted by Nahum)

Fairbairn (who paid 350 guineas) could not bear the woman's expression and persuaded Hunt to soften it; Hunt: 'the possessors, feeling that the expression of the girl was painful, persuaded me to change it'

In spring 1856 Hunt worked on the head while suffering from fever, before the picture went to the Birmingham Society of Artists; on 16 April 1857 he wrote to Edward Lear: 'I think that I have materially bettered it now'
In his memoirs (1905) Hunt wrote that the picture was taken back before he was sure, and 'it was never sent to me to make certain that its last state compensated for its first'

Hunt and Annie quarrelled and reconciled; she became involved with the 7th Viscount Ranelagh; Hunt broke off the engagement in 1859; Ranelagh suggested she sue Hunt for breach of promise; Ranelagh's first cousin Captain Thomas Thomson fell in love with her; they married on 23 July 1863 at St Pancras Church

Thomson suggested threatening to give Annie's trunk full of letters from Hunt to the newspapers; Hunt's friends assumed he bought back the letters; Years later Hunt met her on Richmond Hill, 'a buxom matron with a carriage full of children', and learned that she was happily married
Annie Miller died in 1925 at Shoreham-by-Sea, aged 90
Hunt retouched the painting in 1864 and 1886, as his notes in the spandrels (usually covered by the frame) record

titles: It Looks Innocent Until You See Her Hands
The Painter Who Tried to Remake His Model
youtube.description_lead: William Holman Hunt's The Awakening Conscience (1853, Tate Britain) looks like a couple at the piano, until you see her hands: rings on every finger but the wedding finger. She is a kept woman, and a song has just woken her conscience. Hunt painted it in a rented room at Woodbine Villa in St John's Wood, a 'maison de convenance', and his model was Annie Miller, a Chelsea barmaid he had met when she was fifteen and planned to educate and marry. While he was in the Holy Land she sat for Rossetti and danced at Cremorne; the buyer, Thomas Fairbairn, couldn't bear her painful expression and Hunt repainted her face; in 1863 Annie married Captain Thomas Thomson. John Ruskin defended the painting in The Times: 'not a single object in all that room… but it becomes tragical, if rightly read.'
credits: The Awakening Conscience (1853), The Light of the World, Our English Coasts, The Scapegoat, The Finding of the Saviour in the Temple and a self-portrait by William Holman Hunt: public domain, via Wikimedia Commons (Tate; Keble College, Oxford; Lady Lever Art Gallery; Birmingham Museums; and other collections).

Drawings and paintings of Annie Miller by Dante Gabriel Rossetti (Helen of Troy, Hamburger Kunsthalle, photo Ad Meskens, released into the public domain); Rossetti's self-portrait, 1847; John Ruskin and Thomas Combe by John Everett Millais; Augustus Egg, Past and Present No. 1 (Tate); Thomas Moore by Thomas Lawrence; Phiz's illustration for David Copperfield; Phoebus Levin, The Dancing Platform at Cremorne Gardens (London Museum); Viscount Ranelagh by Carlo Pellegrini, Vanity Fair 1870 (Yale Center for British Art); John Robert Cozens, The Thames from Richmond Hill; Oft in the Stilly Night, sheet music, 1826 (Library of Congress); Edward Lear, photograph: public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.
